title: Lord Jesus, receive my spirit (Acts 7:54–8:3)
hookLine: some arguments end with a walkout. this one ends with a crowd covering its ears
tomorrow: who tries to buy what can't be bought?
last: THE MOST HIGH DWELLS NOT IN TEMPLES.

cards: Some arguments end with somebody walking out. This one ends with a crowd covering its ears. Stephen's speech is over, and his hearers, Acts says, are cut to the heart and grind their teeth.
Stephen isn't looking at them anymore. He looks up: "Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of man standing on the right hand of God." They shout, rush him, and drive him out of the city.

And at the edge of the scene, almost in the margin, one detail: "the witnesses laid down their clothes at a young man's feet, whose name was Saul." Then the stones begin. What does a man say with the breath he has left?

teach.b: He prays twice. First: "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." Then he kneels and cries with a loud voice: "Lord, lay not this sin to their charge."
Readers of Luke's Gospel hear an echo. On the cross Jesus prayed, "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do," and at the end, "Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit."

teach.h: THE SAME TWO PRAYERS AS THE CROSS.
teach.b: Stephen prays the same two prayers: one handing over his life, one for the people taking it. And he speaks the first one to Jesus by name. That's today's word, Lord Jesus, said as a last breath.
Then Acts uses the gentlest verb it has: "when he had said this, he fell asleep." Devout men bury him and make great lamentation over him.

Here's the thing to tell a friend tonight: the prayer for his killers doesn't stop the killing. Stephen prays it anyway, while it's happening, not years later when it's safe. Then the story turns to the coats.
"And Saul was consenting unto his death."

Right after, Saul goes house to house, dragging believers off to prison. Stephen asked that this sin not be charged against them, and Saul was standing right there. Acts never says whether Saul heard.
It just leaves his name on the page, and keeps it for later.

how: Some churches remember Stephen on a feast day of his own, and some Christians pray his words, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit, at the end of a life, their own or someone they love.

games.q: Stephen's last moments — tap the pairs.
p: laid their clothes at Saul's feet
lay not this sin to their charge

s: Acts puts Saul by the coats, consenting. it never says he threw a stone.
Stephen's last words ask God to punish his killers
he kneels and cries, Lord, lay not this sin to their charge.
Acts says that Stephen fell asleep
when he had said this, he fell asleep: Acts' gentle word for his death.

games.q: a girl at school keeps mocking your little sister for wearing a cross. your sister asks what she should pray. what fits Stephen's way?
o: pray for the girl by name, now, while it's still happening.
pray only to be protected, and leave the girl out of it.
wait until it stops, then start working on forgiving her.
games.why: Stephen prayed for the people stoning him while the stones were still coming: Lord, lay not this sin to their charge. not later, when it was safe.

practice: Bring to mind someone who has hurt you, or, if that's too heavy today, someone who just makes life harder. Jesus told his followers to "pray for them which despitefully use you."
If you pray, say Stephen's words for that person, quietly, out loud: lay not this sin to their charge. If not, say their name aloud once and wish them no harm.

wordCard.voice: Lord Jesus. The name Stephen calls on as he dies, the way Jesus called on the Father from the cross.

orig.note: Greek: Lord Jesus, the opening of Stephen's prayer in Acts 7:59.

carryVoice: The line to keep: receive my spirit, and the second prayer that came right after it. Rest well.
